title: Challenge: Circular Monotonic Stack

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only circular-monotonic-stack program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
The second pass resolves wraparound answers without duplicating candidates. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `[3,1,2]`, the worked program returns `-1,2,3`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `[1,2,1]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Return each value's next greater value in circular order.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Return each value's next greater value in circular order. On input `[1,2,1]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Traverse indexes twice while storing each unresolved position only once. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. A stack remembers unfinished work in last-in-first-out order; a queue processes work in first-in-first-out order. Say what each stored item still needs. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(n) time · O(n) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Check empty containers, one item, repeated equal values, and the work left in the structure after the input ends. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `-1,8,8,8,8,8,8`. The second pass resolves wraparound answers without duplicating candidates. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: For [1,2,1], the first pass resolves index 0 to 2. The second pass lets index 2 encounter the earlier 2 across the boundary. Value 2 has no greater value anywhere and retains -1.
